Now in this article, we will see some other unusual and fascinating features of the grammar of the French language.

# Going to the Future & Coming from the Past

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The normal way of forming a future tense is using the auxiliary “will” and attaching the verb root after it. For example :

> English : *I will swim* (future)

But there is another way of forming the future tense in English that is used for future events that are going to happen soon from the present (immediate future) and/or if it is very certain (certain future). The way to do this is by conjugating the verb “go” in present continuous tense and then attaching the “to” form of the verb after. For example :

> English : *I am going to swim* (immediate future)

Let us think about it for a while. The phrase “*going to*” is used in this sentence simply as a signal for a future tense, not because there is an actual movement of going involved. I am not going anywhere when I say “*I am going to swim*”. It is just that the verb “*go*” has lost its literal meaning and is now becoming a surrogate for marking the future tense.

The phenomenon where a word loses its literal meaning and assumes a grammatical function (like marking a tense or aspect) is called as **grammaticalisation**.

How did this happen? Turns out in Middle English, this “*going to*” construction was used only when there was an actual movement involved. When a Shakespearean character says something like “*I am going to buy fish*”, it was because the character was actually going somewhere (maybe to the market) to buy fish. Then eventually as English evolved, people generalised the meaning and began to understand and use the “*going to*” construction as a marker for a future tense, forgetting the actual meaning of the verb “*go*”.

In other words, in English, “*going to*” started in Middle English/Early Modern English with literal movement + purpose.

> *I am going to buy fish*   
> =\> originally meant : you’re actually traveling somewhere to buy
> fish).
>
> Over time, it generalised to intention, near-future prediction, and
> even pure futurity without any motion. Eventually, it decoupled from
> literal “going.” Now,
>
> *I am going to buy fish  *
> =\> now : means just a future action, even if you are not actually
> physically going anywhere to buy fish

This is not that surprising and can be seen in many languages where one uses the verb “go” to form an immediate certain future tense. For example :  

> French original : *Je vais nager*  
> Literal translation : I go to swim   
> Actual meaning : I will swim (future tense)
>
>   
> Tamil original : *nāṉ nīnda pōrēṉ*  
> Literal translation : I to-swim go (I go to swim)  
> Actual meaning : I will swim (future tense)

  
Now, I have always thought for a long time. If a construction “I go to swim / I am going to swim” can be used to signify future tense events very near to the current, then by symmetry,

> Go X come (opposites)  
> To X from (opposites)  
> Future X past (opposites)

If we replace the word “*go*” by its opposite “*come*”, the preposition “*to*” by its opposite “*from*”, then we should get the opposite of the immediate future tense which is the immediate past tense (recent past tense).  
  
Turns out this doesn’t happen in English. A sentence like “*I come from swimming*” or “*I am coming from swimming*” is used only when there is a literal coming involved and is not a generic way of forming the recent past tense. English uses another auxiliary verb “*have*” to form its recent past tense by adding the word “just” (eg : *I have just swum*).

But turns out French is symmetric and forms its recent past tense by the symmetric replacement that I hypothesised

> Go =\> come   
> To =\> from

Let us see how French forms its recent past tense and compare it to its immediate future tense.

> French recent past tense :   
> French original : *Je viens de nager*   
> Literal trans : **I come from swimming**
>
> French immediate future tense :   
> French original : *Je vais nager   *
> Literal translation : **I go to-swim**

This was an AHA wonder moment for me !! As expected, in French “*Je viens de nager*” which literally means “*I come from swimming*” means a recent past event like “*I have just swum*”.  
  
English lacks this full grammatical symmetry. “*I am coming from swimming*” stays mostly literal (you’ve physically returned from the pool). English “*going to*” grammaticalised strongly for the future, but the “*coming from*” path didn’t take off the same way. But it did, in French !!

This kind of spatial metaphor for time (future = ahead/in front = going toward; past = behind = coming from) is widespread in languages, rooted in how humans conceptualise time by visualising it in terms of space (you go into the future and come from the past!!) 😃😃

# Reflexive Verbs : Doing to Yourself

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

You would have heard a lot of advice on not to literally translate everything when you are learning a new language. For French too, this holds and one of the examples where it spectacularly fails is when you try to translate this simple sentence “*My name is Rama*” from English to French. Let us first try to literally translate it word by word.

> English =\> French :  
> my =\> *mon*  
> name =\> *nom*  
> is =\> *est*  
> Rama =\> *Rama*

When you translate this literally word by word, you have :

> English original : My name is Rama  
> French literal translation : *~~Mon nom est Rama~~* \*

I have struck the sentence out because despite being grammatically perfect, a Frenchman would never use this sentence to tell his name. How does a Frenchman named Rama tell his name? Turns out it is as follows :

> French original : *Je m’ appelle Rama*  
> Literal translation : I me call Rama (I call myself Rama)  
> Normal translation : My name is Rama
>
> Word by word analysis : French =\> English  
> *Je* =\> I  
> *Me* (*m*’) =\> me / myself  
> *appelle* =\> call

So, a Frenchman would literally say “*I call me (myself) Rama*” to say what an English man says “*My name is Rama*”. This is an interesting matter of stylistic difference and illustrates the peril of literal translation and that how learning a new language is much more than learning a set of words and grammar rules. But this sentence has introduced us to a special class of verbs in French called “**reflexive verbs**” (prominaux).

Let us compare two sentences in French :

> French Original : *Je **m’** appelle Rama*  
> Literal English : I call myself Rama  
> Actual English : My name is Rama
>
> French Original : *J’ appelle Rama*   
> Literal English : I call Rama  
> Actual English : I call Rama (I call someone else called Rama)

Do you see what happens when the word for “me/myself” (which is “*me*” in French) is removed? The meaning changes from “I call myself Rama” to “I call Rama” (call someone else who is Rama). Let us do this for some other verbs.

> Waking yourself =\> Waking someone else
>
> French original : *Je **me** lève*  
> Literal English : I rise myself   
> Actual English : I get up (e.g. from bed in the morning)
>
> French original : *Je leve mon bébé*  
> Literal English : I rise my baby   
> Actual English : I get my baby up (I wake up my baby from bed)

Some more examples are shown.

> Relaxing yourself =\> Relaxing someone else
>
> French original : *Je **me** relaxe*  
> Literal English : I relax myself   
> Actual English : I relax
>
> French original : *Je relaxe mon bébé*  
> Literal English : I relax my baby   
> Actual English : I make my baby relax

> Bathing yourself =\> Bathing someone else
>
> French original : *Je **me** lave*  
> Literal English : I wash myself   
> Actual English : I bathe
>
> French original : *Je lave mon bébé*  
> Literal English : I bath my baby   
> Actual English : I make my baby bathe

> Stopping yourself =\> Stopping someone else
>
> French original : *Je **m’** arrête*  
> Literal English : I stop myself   
> Actual English : I stop (myself)
>
> French original : *J’ arrête ma voiture*  
> Literal English : I stop my car  
> Actual English : I stop my car

What is exactly happening here? Before going further, it is useful to learn an important grammatical concept regarding verbs.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ReZW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fffde5319-9819-44a9-9458-2d228c29645a_2048x1105.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ReZW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fffde5319-9819-44a9-9458-2d228c29645a_2048x1105.png "Screenshot 2025-11-07 at 11.18.03.png")

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In English, verbs like “stop” and “relax” that are used either transitively or intransitively have the same form in English. But in French, some of these verbs have a distinct form for their intransitive variants. When I want to say “I relax” intransitively (I relax myself), you put the subject itself as the object and say “I me relax” in French but when you use the verb transitively in English as in “I relaxe my baby”, you do not put the subject itself as the object and instead put the object after the verb. So, what is happening here is that French is using different forms for the same English verb depending on whether it is used transitively or intransitively.

> Relax (intransitive) =\> Je me relaxe (I relax)  
> Relax (transitive) =\> Je relaxe … (I relax .. someone else)

Even in Tamil and other Indian languages, transitive and intransitive verbs are distinguished grammatically.

For example :

> English : It **opens** (intransitive) / I **open** the door
> (transitive)  
> Hindi : *Yah **khultā** hai* / *Maiṃ dvār **kholtā** hūṃ*
>
> English : He **joined** (intransitive) / He **joined** them  
> Tamil : *Avaṉ **cērndāṉ** / Avaṉ avarkaḷai **cērttāṉ***
>
> English : I stop (intransitive) / I stop my car (transitive)  
> French : *Je **m’** **arrête*** / *J’ **arrête** ma voiture*

French simply adds “myself / yourself / ..” to reflect intransitivity and mark it distinctly for some verbs. That is all. But, this story does not stop here.

For example, consider the French verb “souvenir” which technically means “to remember”. But, when it used reflexively, we have :

> French original : *Je **me** souviens*  
> Literal English : I remember myself (does not make sense literally)  
> Actual English : I recollect

There is no transitive counterpart for this verb in French.

> *Je souviens ……*

does not exist in French. French uses many other verbs for the transitive form in this case and uses the “*souvenir*” verb only in the reflexive manner to mean to recollect which means to remember to oneself.

Thus, French reflexive verbs originated as ordinary intransitive forms of transitive verbs whose action is directed back toward the subject (”wash oneself”, “stop oneself”, “call oneself”). But, over time, however, many became fixed expressions whose meanings are no longer fully predictable from the literal reflexive sense. Thus reflexive verbs form an important grammatical category of their own in French.

# Pronouns Switch Places

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In English and many other languages, we know that short words like he/him/she/her/it/I/you replace nouns. And when they replace it, they take the exact place where the noun would have been. For example :

> Without pronoun : I want **a croissant**  
> With pronoun : I want **it** (it = croissant)

But in French, when the pronoun is the object of a verb, it suddenly comes before the verb, despite normal object nouns coming after the verb. For example, let us see the same sentence-pair above in French:

> Without pronoun : *Je veux **un croissant*** =\> I want **a
> croissant**  
> With pronoun : *Je **le** veux* (le = croissant) =\> I want **it**

As a more popular example, the French phrase that is used to say “please” is “*s’ il vous plaît*” which literally means “if it pleases you”. But note that here “you” (French : “***vous***”) is the object of this phrase, it comes before the verb.

> With pronoun : *s’il **vous** plait* =\> If it pleases you (pronoun
> object comes before the verb)

But, when it comes to the imperative (command verbs), this peculiarity vanishes. The object comes after the verb even if it is a pronoun. As an example :

> French : *Excusez **moi***  
> Literally : Excuse **me**  
> (Here, the object “me” (“moi” in French) comes after the verb like
> normally)

# You alway eat “SOME” bread in France

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One of the first things that surprises English speakers learning French is that French often refuses to let a noun stand by itself. This is the topic that still frustrates me a lot in French grammar and where I make a huge load of mistakes.

Consider the simple sentence “I eat bread” where the quantity is unspecified. How does this come about in French? Let us see below. Note that the word “***du***” in French means “of the” in French literally.

> French original : *Je mange **du** pain*  
> Literal translation : I eat **of-the** bread  
> Actual meaning : I eat bread

A beginner would naturally translate the sentence “I eat bread” into French wrongly as :

> French (wrong) : *~~Je mange pain~~*

But this is impossible in French. The noun *pain* (”bread”) needs a special article before it when it occurs with the verb “*manger*” (to eat). In this case, that article is *du*.

Similarly, some more examples :

> French original : *Je bois **du** vin*  
> Literal translation : I drink **of-the** wine  
> Actual meaning : I drink wine

> French original : *Je mange **de la** viande*  
> Literal translation : I eat *of-the* meat  
> Actual meaning : I eat meat

> French original : *Je bois **de** **l**’ eau*  
> Literal translation : I drink **of-the** water  
> Actual meaning : I drink water

What exactly is this mysterious *du*, *de la*, and *de l’*? The answer is that French distinguishes between two kinds of nouns. They are :

Countable discrete things (things you can count individually)

Examples: apple (one apple, two apple, three apples), pear, pen, box

Uncountable continuous substances (things that are treated as a mass)

Examples: bread, wine, water, meat

These are not normally counted as individual units. Instead, we take a portion of them. When we say “I eat bread”, what we really mean is “I eat some portion of a lump of bread”. Likewise, when we say “I drink wine”, what is really happening is “I drink some portion of a liquid mass of wine”. English usually leaves this concept unspoken and understood from context (of course, we are always eating some portion of a lump of bread and drinking some portion of a liquid mass of wine, they obviously do not come naturally in discrete lumps!). However, French does not and insists on marking this idea explicitly using what is called the *partitive article*.

The word “partitive” comes from the idea of a “part” of something.

> *du* = (some) of the → for masculine nouns)  
> *de la* = (some) of the → for feminine nouns)  
> *de l’* = (some) of the → for nouns that start in a vowel

Thus, French sentences like “*Je mange du pain*” (I eat some bread), “*Je bois du vin*” (I drink some wine), “*Je mange de la viande*” (I eat some meat), “*Je bois de l’eau*” (I drink some water) have a fascinating origin.

The French word *du* is historically a contraction of: de + le = du

which literally means: of + the = of the

Thus: Je bois du vin

originally meant something closer to: I drink of the wine.

Similarly: de la = of the (feminine)

The construction gradually lost its literal meaning and became a grammatical marker indicating an unspecified quantity of an uncountable continuous substance! In other words, another case of grammaticalisation! This leads to this interesting difference between English and French.

French feels uncomfortable talking about an uncountable substance without indicating that only a portion of it is involved. The language therefore inserts this partitive article (du, de la, de l’). In fact, French often sounds as though it is constantly saying “some” where English remains silent.

This is another example of a broader lesson that I have repeatedly encountered while learning French. Languages often force speakers to make distinctions that other languages leave implicit. English allows me to simply say “*I eat bread*.” French insists that I tell it whether I am eating a particular bread (*le pain*) or merely some bread (*du pain*). What English leaves unsaid, French frequently chooses to express explicitly.

# Sports, Music, and Other Things You Cannot Pour into a Glass

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At this point, I thought I had understood the French partitive article. It is used for substances like bread, wine, water, and meat where English silently implies the word “some”. Everything seemed straightforward. Then I encountered the following sentence:

> French original : *Je fais **du** tennis*  
> Literal translation : I do some tennis  
> Actual meaning : I play tennis

Wait a minute. Tennis is not bread. It is not wine. It is not even a substance (let alone countable or uncountable). Nobody can pour tennis into a glass or cut off a piece of tennis and eat it. It is an abstract action noun. Why then is the partitive article *du* suddenly appearing here?

The answer again, is that the French partitive article has gradually expanded beyond its original role of referring to an unspecified quantity of a physical substance. In modern French, it is also used in many expressions involving activities, sports, hobbies, disciplines, and artistic pursuits. For example:

> French original : *Je fais du **football***   
> Literal translation : I do some football  
> Actual meaning : I play football

> French original : *Je fais **de la** musique*  
> Literal translation : I do some music  
> Actual meaning : I make music / I play music

> French original : *Je fais **de la** danse*  
> Literal translation : I do some dancing  
> Actual meaning : I dance

Notice something interesting. The common factor is not the noun itself. The noun *tennis* does not always require *du*, unlike the noun *pain* (bread). For example:

> French original : J’aime le tennis  
> Literal translation : I like the tennis  
> Actual meaning : I like tennis

Here there is no partitive article and we have instead the definite article “the” that is used to denote a general category as a whole. Instead, the partitive article here appears specifically with the verb *faire* (”to do”) when talking about participating in an activity.

> French original : *Je fais **du** tennis*  
> Literal translation : I do some tennis
>
> French original : *Je fais **de la** musique*  
> Literal translation : I do some music

In other words, French conceptualises participation in an activity as doing some amount of that activity. Just as one can eat some bread or drink some wine, one can also do some tennis or do some music. Imagine the action of tennis as one giant lump and every individual person doing that action is partaking in a lump of it **😃 😃.**

This happens in lots of other verb phrases and in other contexts too. Some examples are shown below where English simply would omit the partitive article.

- *avoir **du** courage* (literally in French : to have **some**
  courage)

- *montrer **du** talent* (literally in French : to show **some**
  talent)

- *avoir **de** **la** patience* (literally in French : to have **some**
  patience)

- *avoir **de la** chance* (literally in French : to have **some** luck)

- *avoir **de l’**imagination* (literally in French : to have **some**
  imagination)

It is also used in the context of playing musical instruments.

> French Original : *Je joue **du** violon*  
> Literal English : I play **of-the** violin (I play some violin)  
> Actual English : I play violin

Apparently French wants us to imagine that when you are playing violin, you are just doing a small part of all the possible playings that can be done with a violin!!

French often uses the partitive with weather too !

- *Il y a **du** vent* (literally in French : There is **some** wind →
  It is windy)

Again this is treated as mass. What verb phrases use partitive article for abstract nouns is a pain in the ass for a French learner and I am still struggling to navigate the labyrinthe of partitive articles in French. Wish me luck in this regard (or as the French would say : *Bonne chance!*!)

This was another fascinating example of further grammaticalisation for me. Originally, the partitive article referred to taking a part or portion of some physical substance. Over time, the same grammatical construction expanded into more abstract domains. Today, a French speaker can use the same structure for bread, wine, music, photography, football, dancing, and countless other activities. Yet another reminder that grammar is full of old ideas that have escaped their original meanings and taken on entirely new lives.

# Compulsion becomes Future

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

How does French form the normal future tense? Let us compare two sentences in French.

> French Original : J’ ai   
> English Translation : I have
>
> French Original : Je parlerai (parler + ai)  
> Literal English : I to-speak have (I have to speak)  
> English Actual : I will speak
>
> parler = to speak  
> ai = have (I have)

Thus, we see that the historically “parler + ai = speak + have” originally in French, meant something like “I have to speak” or “I have speaking to do”. This is again a beautiful grammaticalisation story where the verb “ai” (to have) has lost its literal meaning (in the sense of possession) and has now become a marker of the future tense.

# Why such a big word for TODAY and a sophisticated YES?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The French word for “today” is so big and it is “*aujourd’hui*”. It can be literally split up and analysed as :

- *aujourd’hui* = *au* *jour* *de* *hui*

Turns out “hui” was the Old French word for 'today’ and hence the phrase ‘*au joure de hui*’ originally meant literally “on the day of today”. The funny thing is that *hui* already meant “today.” This kind of repetition is not that uncommon and can be found in English too as in “chai tea” and “naan bread”.

French also has two words for YES, which are : *oui*, *si*.

The “oui” is the normal “yes” to affirm a positive statement whereas “si” is the “yes” to deny a negative statement. This special affirmative used to contradict a negative statement fascinates learners like me. Example :

> Tu parles français ? (Do you speak French?)  
> Oui ! (Yes, I do!!)
>
> Tu ne parles pas français ? (Do you not speak French?)  
> Si ! (Yes, I do!!)

How Can “Person” Mean “Nobody”?

# The French Negation Marker : Ne ….. Pas

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To negate a statement in French, you put a “**ne**“ before the verb and “**pas**“ after it.

> Positive Statement :   
> French original : *Je parle Français*  
> Literal English : I speak French
>
> Negation :   
> French original : *Je **ne** parle **pas** Français*  
> Literal English : I **don’t** speak French

The marker “**ne**” is very familiar and is a standard negation marker in all Indo-European languages (e.g. English “no(t)” , Hindi “na”). What strikes as peculiar is the word “pas”. The word “**pas**“ actually literally means “step”.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fSzx!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F99c4e00e-1211-4c76-8c5c-7d33ca697d76_1382x308.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fSzx!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F99c4e00e-1211-4c76-8c5c-7d33ca697d76_1382x308.png)

So, the word “pas” means both “step” and a negative marker. Is this just a coincidence or there is something deeper to probe here? In Old French, this phenomenon used to occur only with verbs of motion where it literally meant “step” for emphatic negation like :

> French original : *Je **ne** marche \***pas**\**   
> Literal English : I don’t walk a \***step**\*   
> Meaning in Old French : I don’t walk at all , not even a step

This derived from the Latin “*nec…..passum*” meaning “*not……a step*”. This “*ne…pas*” construction in Old French was used as an emphatic negation with only verbs of motion in sentences like “I do not walk a step”, “I do not go a step” , etc. As time went on, French people started using this emphatic “**pas**“ more often casually. Then, it also began to be used along with other verbs as it was begun to be understood as generic sign of negation rather an emphatic negation of verbs of motion.

Old French had even more emphatic negators to be used with various kinds of verbs , some of which were:

- *pas* = step (we already saw this)

- *point* = point

- mie = crumb

- goutte = drop

Originally one could say things like:

> French original : *Je ne bois goutte*
>
> English translation : I do not drink a drop
>
> French original : *Je ne mange mie*
>
> English translation : I do not eat a crumb

Eventually, the word “***pas*****”** won the competition to become the standard negator for all verbs in modern French.

In fact, in modern colloquial French, the negative marker “*ne*“ is disappearing from usage, and only “pas” is seen as the negative marker. So they only say

> Colloquial French : *Je parle **pas** Francais  *
> English meaning : I don’t speak French”

It is so funny. By just seeing modern French negative marker “pas” meaning “step” , you would never guess why it doubles as a negation marker. This is an interesting example of how much words and their meanings in a language can change with time.

# A Person is a Nobody in France !

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After I thought “pas” was enough and it was just one odd word that seemed to have abandoned its original meaning to become a negation marker, I encountered another curious word that seemed equally schizophrenic. Consider the following French sentence:

> French original : *Je vois une **personne***  
> Literal translation : I see a **person**  
> Actual meaning : I see a **person**

Nothing unusual so far. The word *personne* clearly means “person”. Now consider this:

> French original : *Je **ne** vois **personne***  
> Literal translation : I do **not** see **person**  
> Actual meaning : I see **nobody**
>
> ***ne….personne*** **= not … person =** nobody

Wait a minute. The same word that previously meant “person” now seems to mean exactly the opposite: “nobody”. How can one word mean both “a person” and “no person”? To understand this, we need to go back in time. Historically, *personne* simply meant “person”, deriving ultimately from the Latin word *persona*. In Old French, one could say things equivalent to:

> French original : *Je **ne** vois **personne***  
> Literal translation : I do **not** see a **person**

Here, the word *personne* still retained its ordinary meaning of “person”. The negation was carried entirely by the word *ne*. The sentence therefore literally meant: “I do not see a person”. In English, we can still construct similar sentences like : “did not see a person there”. Notice that “person” itself is not negative. The negativity comes from the word “not”. Over time, however, French speakers began to use *personne* so frequently in negative sentences that listeners started associating the word itself with negation.

The evolution of meanings went something like this:

I do not see **a person** → I do not see **any person** → I see **no person** → I see **nobody**

Eventually, the word became reinterpreted as a negative word in its own right. Thus modern French speakers understand:

> *Je **ne** vois **personne***

not as:

> ~~I do~~ **~~not~~** ~~see a~~ **~~person~~**

but as:

> I see nobody.

The same word therefore ended up with two meanings depending on context (in this case negation):

Positive context:

> French original : ***Une personne** arrive*  
> Literal translation : **A person** arrives  
> Meaning : **A person** is arriving

Negative context:

> French original : ***Personne** **n**’arrive*  
> Literal translation : **Person** arrives-**not**  
> Meaning : **Nobody** is arriving

This phenomenon is not unique to *personne*. Several French negative words underwent exactly the same evolution. For example:

> French original : *Je **ne** vois **rien***  
> Literal translation : I do **not** see a **thing**  
> Actual meaning : I see **nothing**
>
> ***ne….rien*** **= not … thing =** nothing

The word *rien* originally meant “**thing**” or “**anything**” and comes from the Latin *rem* (”thing”). Similarly:

> French original : *Je **ne** vais **jamais** là-bas*  
> Literal translation : I do **not** go **ever** there  
> Actual meaning : I **never** go there
>
> ***ne … jamais*** **= not ….. ever =** never

The word *jamais* originally meant something like “**ever**” rather than “**never**”. Thus:

> rien  
> original meaning : thing  
> modern negative meaning : *ne…..rien* = nothing
>
> personne  
> original meaning : person  
> modern negative meaning : *ne…personne* = nobody
>
> jamais  
> original meaning : ever  
> modern negative meaning : *ne….jamais* = never
>
> Eventually, the “ne” was neglected and the words on the right were
> understood as the actual negative markers !!!

Does this story sound familiar? It should. Earlier we saw that *pas* originally meant “step”.

> French original : *Je ne marche pas*  
> Literal translation : I do **not** walk a **step**  
> Meaning then : I do not walk at all  
> Meaning now : I do not walk

The word *pas* was originally just an ordinary noun that meant “step”. Through repeated use in negative contexts, it gradually acquired a negative meaning of its own and it swallowed the role of the negative marker “ne”. Exactly the same thing happened with:

> pas = step → not  
> personne = person → nobody  
> rien = thing → nothing  
> jamais = ever → never

All of them began life as ordinary words. All of them were repeatedly used alongside the old negation marker *ne*. And all of them eventually became associated with negation themselves.

In modern colloquial French, this historical process has gone so far that the original negation marker *ne* is often omitted entirely:

> French Colloquial : *Je vois **personne***  
> English meaning : I see **nobody !!!**
>
> French Colloquial : *Je vois **rien***  
> English meaning : I see **nothing**
>
> French Colloquial : *J’ai **jamais** vu ça*  
> English meaning : I have **never** seen that

The ancient negation marker *ne* is slowly disappearing, while the words that once merely accompanied it are taking over its job. This is perhaps one of the most beautiful examples of how languages evolve. A word meaning “step” becomes “not”. A word meaning “person” becomes “nobody”. A word meaning “thing” becomes “nothing”. A word meaning “ever” becomes “never”. Languages are full of such ghosts of earlier meanings, hiding in plain sight.

French negation is not one story but many parallel stories. The language repeatedly recruited ordinary nouns and adverbs like : step, person, thing, ever, etc.. to reinforce negation. Over centuries these words themselves became negative words, gradually pushing the original negation marker *ne* into retirement and absorbing its meaning in that generalised context

# Latin Persona to French Personne

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Given that we have seen the word “personne” that means “person” normally but also can mean “no one” or “nobody”, what was the original meaning of the Latin word “persona” that gives the French word “person” and English “person”?

he English word “person” ultimately derives from the Latin “persona”. In classical Latin, however, “persona” did not mean “individual human being” as it does today in most modern European languages. Instead, it originally meant “mask”: specifically the mask worn by an actor in Greco-Roman theatre.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1F12!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad636e19-7f7d-4ab9-882d-d12b6a03b8d5_1138x954.jpeg)

![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1F12!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad636e19-7f7d-4ab9-882d-d12b6a03b8d5_1138x954.jpeg "Image")

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

  
In ancient theatrical performances, a single actor often portrayed multiple characters by changing masks, and the mask itself was called a “persona”. The etymology is likely from either the Etruscan word “phersu” (mask) or possibly related to the idea of sound (sona) projecting “through” (per) the mouth opening. The standard Latin phrase “***dramatis personae***” literally in Latin means “the masks of the drama” that still appears at the beginning of play scripts.

This theatrical term proved unexpectedly useful centuries later when Christian theologians in the Latin-speaking West grappled with one of the central mysteries of their faith: how it could be legitimate to worship Father, Son (Jesus), and Holy Spirit as God while insisting there is only one God. The classic summary of the apparent paradox, often attributed to St. Augustine, runs as follows where he summarises the Christian doctrine of the trinity as follows :  
  
- The Father is God.   
- The Son (Jesus) is God.   
- The Holy Spirit is God.   
- The Father is not the Son.   
- The Son is not the Holy Spirit.   
- The Holy Spirit is not the Father.   
- There is only one God.  
  
Early Christian heresies such as Arianism had tried to resolve the tension by subordinating the Son (and sometimes the Spirit) to the Father—making Jesus a created being, albeit being the most exalted among creation. Orthodox theologians rejected this, insisting on the full equality and co-eternality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet if the three are truly distinct and each fully God, how are Christians monotheists and not tritheists (worshippers of three gods)?  
  
Greek-speaking theologians in the East primarily solved the problem by distinguishing between one divine “***ousia***” (substance or essence) and three “***hypostases***” (individual subsistences). In the Latin West, however, the available technical vocabulary in philosophy was more limited. The churchfather **Tertullian** (c. 160–220 AD), one of the first to write Christian theology in Latin, introduced the formula “una substantia – tres personae” (“one substance – three personae”). Here “persona” was consciously borrowed from its theatrical sense: just as a single actor can assume different masks to play different roles, the one God eternally “acts” in three distinct roles or personae - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without ceasing to be one God.  
  
Thus:  
- The Father is the transcendent source and originator.   
- The Son is the same God incarnate on earth for the salvation of humanity.   
- The Holy Spirit is the same God actively inspiring and sanctifying believers.  
  
When English-speaking Christians today say God is “one Being in three Persons,” the word “Person” is translating the Latin “persona” - a term that originally meant something ordinary like a theatrical mask. Over the centuries, as the theological usage became dominant, “persona” gradually took on the richer meaning of a distinct center of identity, and from there it entered the Romance languages (French : personne, Spanish and Italian : persona, etc.) and eventually English as our modern word “person”. And it now also means “nobody” in French !!! Language and theology can sometimes couple together and take fascinating turns.
